text: {"answer": "The evidence suggests daily vitamin D supplementation is worthwhile for adults who are deficient, but not clearly necessary for those with adequate levels. Supporting passages report that daily supplementation corrects deficiency and improves bone mineral density in adults with low baseline serum levels [vitamin_d#0], and that muscle strength and fall rates improve in deficient populations [vitamin_d#3]. A meta-analysis reports a modest fracture benefit in older adults when vitamin D is combined with calcium [vitamin_d#1]. Contradicting evidence is substantial. A Cochrane review found no reduction in all-cause mortality in adults who were not deficient at baseline [vitamin_d#5], and the VITAL trial, with 25871 participants, found no significant effect on cardiovascular events or cancer [vitamin_d#4]. Routine supplementation in adequate-level populations shows no measurable outcome gain [vitamin_d#6]. High doses have been linked to hypercalcaemia and, in some trials, higher fall risk [vitamin_d#7]. Observational links to immune benefits [vitamin_d#2] are weaker than trial evidence. Overall, testing status matters, and routine daily use for all adults is not well supported.", "confidence": 62, "one_line": "Daily vitamin D helps deficient adults, but routine use in those with adequate levels shows no clear benefit and possible harms at high doses."}
